intro: Brahms’s First Symphony begins with timpani hammering C while strings climb and winds pull downwards. The Czech National Symphony Orchestra plays a movement whose stern opening finally comes to rest in a quiet C major.

sections.label: Intro · Timpani C, strings climbing
sections.mNote: Rising strings press against descending winds

sections.label: A · Allegro: violins climb through the chord
sections.mNote: Violin arpeggios above the opening’s three-note ascent

sections.label: Dev · The violin theme in B major
sections.mNote: The arpeggio moves to a new key

sections.label: Link · Bass rising by semitones
sections.mNote: Horn rhythms and wind phrases gather above the climbing bass

sections.mNote: C minor returns without a pause

sections.mNote: Meno allegro leads towards quiet C-major chords

cues.title: Timpani hold their ground
cues.text: Timpani hammer C. Violins and cellos climb by semitones while winds and violas pull downwards. The double basses and contrabassoon reinforce the drumbeats: the floor stays put while everything above it strains in opposite directions.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, bars 1–8, Simrock first edition (1877), p. 3; Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Karlsruhe, November 1876
cues.text: On 4 November 1876, Otto Dessoff conducts the première in Karlsruhe. Brahms is forty-three. Two serenades, a piano concerto, the German Requiem and the Haydn Variations are already behind him; his First Symphony has taken much longer to reach the platform.
cues.evidence: Première, age and earlier orchestral works: Marc Mandel, Boston Symphony programme note. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: The Allegro takes flight
cues.text: The Allegro begins with a low C and the introduction’s rising semitones, now quickened. First violins climb through an arpeggio above throbbing inner strings. Cellos and bassoons keep the three-note ascent moving underneath.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, bars 38–51; Hansen’s score guide describes the opening motto and violin theme. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An oboe over murmuring strings
cues.text: The gentler second theme belongs to the oboe, then the clarinets, in E♭ major. Violas repeat notes beneath it. The melody’s sighs and small chromatic steps recall the introduction, though the oboe now lets them sing.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, second-theme group, bars 130–156; Hansen’s score guide. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The arpeggio lands in B
cues.text: The violin arpeggio reappears in B major, a semitone below the home keynote. Soon the strings subside into tremolo and a bassoon takes up the phrase. B major darkens into B minor.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, development, bars 189–204; Hansen’s score guide. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Simrock grows impatient
cues.text: On 22 February 1873, the publisher Fritz Simrock writes to Brahms: “Aren’t you doing anything anymore? Am I not to have a symphony from you in ’73 either?” Three more years pass before the First is finished.
cues.evidence: Fritz Simrock to Brahms, 22 February 1873, quoted by Marc Mandel in the Boston Symphony programme note. https://www.bso.org/works/symphony-no-1-in-c-minor

cues.title: The bass begins to climb
cues.text: After a long wait on G, the bass begins climbing by semitones. Horns repeat the short-note rhythm; oboes and clarinets answer with descending phrases. Each repetition pushes the bass a little higher, until trumpets and timpani join the insistence.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, extended retransition, bars 273–339; Hansen describes the G pedal, chromatic bass ascent and alternating horn and wind figures. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: C minor without a pause
cues.text: The rising semitones carry straight into the return. The first violins recover their arpeggio in C minor while the orchestra is still in full motion. Brahms cuts away part of the opening group and moves on sooner than before.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, recapitulation, bars 340 onwards; elided motto and shortened first group described by Hansen. http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Plucked strings, softer semitones
cues.text: Hammered thirds become quiet plucked notes beneath a long violin phrase. Later, Meno allegro slows the music, and winds and strings pass the rising semitones between them. The arpeggio finally opens into C major; the last chords are soft.
cues.evidence: First Symphony, I, coda, bars 475–511; Meno allegro at bar 495 and C-major ending. Hansen, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A plucked G releases the Allegro
transitions.to: A · Allegro: violins climb through the chord
transitions.how: The cellos finish the introduction with a quiet plucked G, the dominant of C. The Allegro answers with a low C and quickened rising semitones in the winds. First violins then launch their arpeggio above the same semitones in cellos and bassoons.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, I, bars 33–51; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: A whole tone leads to B
transitions.from: A · Allegro: violins climb through the chord
transitions.to: Dev · The violin theme in B major
transitions.how: The closing descent takes a whole step down to B. Strings begin the first theme’s arpeggio in B major, supported by wind chords. Eight bars later the violins turn to tremolo; a solo bassoon and low strings continue the theme as the harmony moves into B minor.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, I, second ending and development, bars 189–204; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: The G pedal starts to move
transitions.from: Dev · The violin theme in B major
transitions.how: The repeated G in the bass has held the dominant in place. Now low strings begin a rising sequence, moving by semitones beneath horn rhythms and answering oboe and clarinet phrases. The strings climb higher and the crescendo continues until the bass settles back onto the dominant.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, I, bars 273–320; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: The semitones carry straight through
transitions.how: The wind semitones and rushing strings continue through the join. Brahms omits the low C that announced the exposition; the rising motto enters within the ongoing sequence. The violin arpeggios follow in C minor, and the returning first group is compressed.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, I, bars 328–343 and following; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

transitions.title: Hammered thirds become plucked strings
transitions.to: Coda · Plucked strings, then a slower close
transitions.how: The repeated thirds soften into pizzicato accompaniment. Violins stretch the rising semitone figure into a longer phrase over plucked cellos. The coda first cadences in C minor; at Meno allegro, winds and strings exchange the figure above a held C before the final turn to major.
transitions.evidence: First Symphony, I, coda, bars 475–511; Hansen’s score guide, http://www.kellydeanhansen.com/opus68.html.

source.title: Brahms, Symphony No. 1, Simrock first-edition full score, plate 7957 (1877)
source.locator: I. Un poco sostenuto — Allegro — Meno allegro, pp. 3–26; introduction, themes, development, return at bar 340 and coda at bar 475. Bar references follow Kelly Dean Hansen’s score guide.

timeline.note: Violins and cellos climb against descending winds and repeated timpani C.
Plucked string figures answer one another above soft wind harmony.
An oboe begins the quiet phrase near the introduction’s end, supported by other winds.
Cellos take over the oboe’s phrase against quiet upper strings.
Violins climb through arpeggios above the three-note rise in cellos and bassoons.
Oboe begins the E♭-major second theme over repeated viola notes; clarinet follows.
The violin arpeggio starts the development in B major, then winds answer over string tremolo.
The bass climbs by semitones beneath repeated horn rhythms and answering woodwind.
Violins restore the opening Allegro arpeggio in C minor, with wind support.
Plucked thirds accompany a long violin phrase at the start of the coda.
At Meno allegro, winds and strings exchange the three-note chromatic figure.

composer.epithet: He kept his First Symphony waiting until he was forty-three, then began the Second beside an Austrian lake the next summer.
facts: Piano with Otto Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Detmold, 1857–59 · Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64 · Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde, 1872–75
Vienna; summers in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano pieces, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
In the autumn of 1853, a twenty-year-old pianist from Hamburg arrived at the Schumanns’ home in Düsseldorf with an introduction from Joseph Joachim. Johannes Brahms played his own music. Robert Schumann heard a composer of the future and announced him that October in an article called Neue Bahnen — New Paths. Publishers became interested. Brahms now had to live up to a public prophecy before most of the public had heard a note. The young man’s piano sonatas were enormous; the symphonies Schumann expected would take much longer.

Brahms’s father Johann Jakob earned his living playing instruments including the horn and double bass. His mother, Christiane Nissen, was a seamstress. Born in Hamburg in 1833, he studied piano with Otto Cossel and then piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen, who grounded him in Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. He played, arranged and accompanied for money. A tour with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi in 1853 brought him to Joachim, and Joachim sent him on to Düsseldorf.
